title: the daily routine (dinacharya)
hook: a toothbrush, a tongue, a clean shirt: a classical Ayurvedic text treats them as the ground of health

segments.voice: Yesterday closed the three doshas as a way of noticing, not a diagnosis, with one line from the Ashtanga Hridaya: health is the three in balance. Where did you make a small correction toward the middle? Day one thousand two hundred ninety-three.

A toothbrush sits in a cup by the sink. It's one of the least dramatic objects in a home. Nobody photographs it. Nobody thinks of it as part of anything deep. And yet one of Ayurveda's classical texts, the Charaka Samhita, gives real space to exactly this kind of thing: cleaning the teeth, rinsing the mouth, washing, putting on clean clothes. Next to its teaching on the doshas and the body sits a careful description of an ordinary morning. Why would a text about health spend its words there? Today we start a run of days on the daily round.
screen: `A TOOTHBRUSH IN A CUP.` → `A CLASSICAL TEXT, AN ORDINARY MORNING.` → `WHY SPEND WORDS THERE?`

segments.voice: The Sanskrit name is dinacharya. Dina is day. Charya is a way of going about, a conduct. The day's conduct: the daily round. In the Charaka Samhita, the chapter on daily regimen begins with eating in the right measure, and then walks through things anyone would recognize. Caring for the eyes. Cleaning the teeth with a twig. Scraping the tongue. Rinsing the mouth. Oil for the body. A bath. Clean clothes. Paraphrased, but the list really is that plain. Start with the size of it. The text doesn't ask for a heroic month. It asks for this morning, and then the next one. Health, in this picture, is less an event than a texture, woven out of small repeated acts. Then there's repetition, which can be a gift. A routine you don't have to decide every time frees up attention. The teeth get cleaned while the mind is somewhere else, and that's fine. But the text also lists these acts one by one, as if each is worth doing well. So there's an invitation inside the habit: now and then, do the ordinary thing on purpose. And the routine has neighbors. In some Hindu homes the morning also has a bath before worship, a lamp lit, a prayer or a name said. Ayurveda's daily round sits comfortably beside those, and the next days will show how far the texts let it reach, even into how a person speaks to others. None of this is a rule to pass or fail. It's a way of seeing a morning: not as the boring part before life starts, but as a place where life is already being looked after.
screen: `DINA, DAY · CHARYA, CONDUCT` · `TEETH, TONGUE, OIL, BATH, CLOTHES` · `THE DAY IS THE UNIT` · `DO THE ORDINARY THING ON PURPOSE`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: walk through this morning again, slowly. Let the eyes close or soften, and go back to the moment you woke. Then, step by step, the things you did: water, the sink, the mirror, clothes, the door. No judging what's missing. Just see the round you already keep. Then pick one step, a small one, and see yourself doing it tomorrow with full attention, as if it mattered. If you pray, you can give thanks for one ordinary thing in that list. The bell holds the time.
The daily routine. Dinacharya, the day's conduct: small, repeated acts that the classical texts treat as the ground of health. Today's word.
Your line: the daily routine, dinacharya. Today, pick one thing you do every day anyway, and do it once on purpose, slowly, start to finish. Day one thousand two hundred ninety-three.

howItsDone: People who follow Ayurveda keep a morning round described in the classical texts, such as cleaning the teeth, scraping the tongue, rinsing the mouth, oiling the body and bathing, often alongside a family's own morning worship.
